canberra.title: I’m not ready to say goodbye to Colin from Accounts
canberra.snippet: The Australian sense of humour is unique, with its banter-fueled, often put-down nature being its own special breed of comedy that outsid...
canberra.content:
After three seasons and 24 episodes, Colin from Accounts has officially wrapped up. Photo: John Platt.

The Australian sense of humour is unique, with its banter-fueled, often put-down nature being its own special breed of comedy that outsiders struggle to understand.

It’s less about set-up and delivery, and more about sharp wit. That’s exactly why great scripted comedies in Australia are few and far between.

Sure, there have been some great hits like Kath and Kim, Utopia and Fisk in recent years, but few have captured international audiences quite like Colin From Accounts.

Its third and final season has just wrapped up on Foxtel’s streaming service Binge, and it’s safe to say the comedy about a paraplegic dog named Colin and the on-again, off-again nature of his owners, Gordon and Ash, is the best Australian comedy of the decade.

A show that started with Gordon accidentally hitting a stray Colin with his car while being dazed by Ash flashing him as a thank you for letting her cross the road became a very real, very funny story about two people navigating a relationship and owning a dog in Sydney.

Its final season picks up three years after the end of season two, when Gordon’s proposal to Ash at her best friend’s wedding went severely wrong, leading the pair to call it quits.

Gordon has sold a majority stake in his pub. Meanwhile, Ash has become a qualified GP. In a chance encounter where Gordon books a flu shot, the two reluctantly rekindle their former romance, but not without some hiccups along the way.

I can’t stress enough in this review how funny Colin from Accounts is. If you have seen it, you understand; and if you haven’t, watch it and you will.

It’s a simple premise elevated by its incredibly quick-witted writing, wacky ensemble cast, and brilliant lead performers (real-life couple Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer).

While an underlying story runs through the season, each new episode throws Gordon and Ash into a crazy new situation that every real human can at least understand.

Whether it’s being stuck in West Wyalong with an EV out of charge, being uninvited to a strangely themed party but showing up anyway, or even deciding which nursing home to put your aging parent in, each sticky situation is laugh-out-loud funny.

It’s all unashamedly Australian, too. Not in the sense that there are exaggerated accents or caricatures of people-like kangaroos either. It’s the little things like complaining about craft beer, sitting down to watch the NRL and the quick back-and-forth banter with the casual inserts of swears that other cultures would raise an eyebrow at.

There are some minor nitpicks to be had. It did feel like the final season manufactured a bit of drama between Gordon and Ash to extend out the question of whether they will get together.

Some side characters, particularly Gordon’s 2IC at the pub, Chiara and Ash’s best friend Megan, also felt like they had a little less to do this season.

Despite these minor gripes, it didn’t damage the overall product; by the final scene of the final episode, the show stuck the landing so satisfyingly that I felt the need to rewatch the entire show from start to finish.

With the show only being 24 episodes from start to finish, Colin from Accounts knew what it was and how to make audiences laugh without overstaying its welcome.

In turn, we got an amazing comedy series from start to finish that is proving a winner not just here in Australia but over in the US and the UK as well.

All three seasons of Colin from Accounts are now streaming on Binge.

canberra.title: Review stokes fears Yarralumla Primary School will say ‘arrivederci’ to its bilingual program
canberra.snippet: The future of Yarralumla Primary School’s bilingual program is at a crossroads, as the Education Directorate conducts a review of t...
canberra.content:
Yarralumla teaches in English and Italian but the program has fallen away in recent years. Photo: Facebook.

The future of Yarralumla Primary School’s bilingual program is at a crossroads, as the Education Directorate conducts a review of the inner south school.

According to the school website, the “targeted review” will assess how the curriculum is being delivered to ensure it meets the needs of all students, aligns with system requirements, and maintains quality bilingual education.

Yarralumla boasts an Italian language program, in which students learn the Australian curriculum through both English and Italian.

The school says this develops strong communication skills, flexible thinking, and a deep appreciation of other cultures.

“This bilingual learning prepares our students to be confident learners and active global citizens,” Acting Principal Lauren Bruhwiller says.

But in a submission to the review, Independent MLA Thomas Emerson says the school community fears the program will be eroded even more than it has over the past seven years, despite it contributing to above average NAPLAN results.

Mr Emerson is urging the Directorate to ensure any changes are developed with the school community.

“Any move to further reduce or eliminate the Yarralumla Primary School’s bilingual program would worsen, rather than improve, the quality of students’ educational experience,” he says.

Mr Emerson says that since 2019, the program has been progressively weakened, with language proficiency targets downgraded.

He says bilingual education was dropped from the school’s previously-stated vision to “become a beacon bilingual school that learns and cultivates community collaboratively through English and Italian,” and the enrolment pathway that had supported Italian-speaking families to access the school was removed.

Many families chose the school for their children to benefit from its bilingual program.

Enrolments progressively declined year-on-year from a peak in 2021 of 390 to 309 students in 2025, with out-of-area enrolments falling from 46 per cent to 39 per cent.

In February 2026, the school advised parents that core subjects would move to English-only, formally ending the practical 50/50 immersion model.

Mr Emerson says the Directorate advised the school community that government policy requires English and mathematics instruction to be delivered in English, but he believes other language immersion schools in the ACT have received an exemption, enabling them to deliver at least half of instruction in another language.

“It is clear there is real demand for a genuine 50/50 bilingual model for Yarralumla Primary School,” the submission says.

“Many families have written to my office, indicating they specifically chose the school as they wanted their children to access the language immersion program.

“Enrolment data shows families are willing to travel for their children to access this program, and the NAPLAN results suggest the model strengthens academic performance.”

Mr Emerson says the school’s experience and the review raises concerns about the ACT Government’s commitment to language education.

“As the nation’s capital with a significant international and diplomatic workforce , the Directorate’s apparent declining support for language education does not meet community expectations, nor does it support Canberra’s future workforce needs and opportunities,” he says.

Mr Emerson also urged the Directorate to consult more fully with families about the future of the bilingual program, highlighting the lack of time families had to make submissions to the review before the 25 August deadline.

The school’s P&C Association said immersive bilingual education provided students with valuable language, cultural and cognitive benefits that could support learning throughout their lives.

“The P&C sees the review as an important chance for government to listen to families and ensure these opportunities continue to thrive,” it said.

The teaching of languages is an ongoing issue for Canberra schools, with qualified teachers hard to come by.

canberra.title: From painted toes to sourdough, how little wins bring calm to a life of chaos
canberra.snippet: If you’re a ‘Type A’ person, this article is not for you. And you’re probably not reading it. You’re at the gym, meal preppin...
canberra.content:
Can something as simple as a tidy sock drawer change your life? Photo: Carrie Allen.

If you’re a ‘Type A’ person, this article is not for you.

And you’re probably not reading it. You’re at the gym, meal prepping, or head down in your calendar setting up your ideal work week.

I honestly don’t know what Type A people do on a Sunday evening, but it’s probably not doom-scrolling, re-watching favourite comfort shows, or staring forlornly into a pile of unsorted clothes, questioning if they were on their way to or from the laundry.

As a person whose prefrontal cortex operates in fits and starts, this is closer to my reality.

I wouldn’t necessarily label myself Type B, though. I’m more akin to Alphabet Soup.

My organisational prowess appears at random, usually triggering major tasks like a total wardrobe rehaul. Unfortunately, my enthusiasm often abandons me halfway through, leaving me adrift in a sea of loosely categorised clothing for weeks, until the wind changes once more.

That said, I’ve found a few simple solutions to curb the chaos and regain a sense of control.

Professional organisers like Marie Kondo have built entire empires on the premise that seemingly small changes – as simple as re-organising our sock drawer – can have a mega impact on how we feel.

Celebrated US Admiral William H McRaven wrote an entire book on the impact of such small achievements. The book is literally called Make Your Bed.

In it, he says: “It was my first task of the day, and doing it right was important. It demonstrated my discipline. It showed my attention to detail, and at the end of the day it would be a reminder that I had done something well, something to be proud of, no matter how small the task.”

They may be illusions (or delusions), but these tiny tasks send happy messages to my brain – about systems, routine, law and order – and keep me feeling calm and capable.

1. Fresh flowers

Though many (read: my husband) view them as a waste of money, I believe fresh flowers pay for themselves by disrupting dull spaces and creating an aura of smug satisfaction. Maybe that intangible ROI is why they send such a potent signal. They say: Hey, I have good taste and at least $50 of disposable income.

Unfortunately, what I never seem to have is an appropriate vase, which is why my last bunch spent two weeks perched unceremoniously in a disused blender – greatly diffusing the air of superiority.

2. Sourdough and a bowl of lemons

As a feeder, a well-stocked fridge or pantry generally gives me good feels.

But certain menu items somehow convince me I’m on top of life. For me, it’s a loaf of locally produced sourdough and a burgeoning bowl of citrus fruit. No further questions, please.

3. Clean windows

A cruel irony indeed that my least favourite domestic chore yields one of my favourite feelings.

When you can look upon the world without squinting past dead bugs, pollen dust and miscellaneous mystery stains, you know you’ve made it. It’s like giving your mind a good Windex.

4. Tidy Tupperware

Tupperware rage is a universal language. Everyone thinks they have an adequate system in place, but none of us does. We are all at the mercy of the Tupperware Gods, who smite us with lost lids, lid oversupply and – occasionally- completely foreign lids you’ve never seen before in your life.

But once in a blue moon, right after our annual lid-sorting ceremony, I feel the warm glow of lid parity and know that all is right in the world.

5. Painted Toenails

I genuinely don’t understand how people keep their nails manicured.

Anytime I’ve attempted this level of grooming, within 24 hours I’m more chipped than my Dad’s 70s-born Datsun. But toenails? That paintwork lasts!

Painted toenails feel extra. They’re giving. In summer, I feel like an extra on Home and Away, and even when concealed, these dainty digits hold a hidden superpower. They give me a quiet confidence nobody can quite place. People probably assume I have confidence, conviction or strength of character. Nope. It’s pink glitter toes.

Whether I’m genuinely kicking goals or not, these are the little maneuvers I’ve discovered that make me feel closer to “winning”.

What are your tiny triumphs?

canberra.title: How a South Coast community is saving women’s lives – on the other side of the world
canberra.snippet: How does a woman who lives in a comfortable seaside community like Malua Bay on the NSW South Coast know what women in a Masaai village i...
canberra.content:
For 10 years Sharlene Cohen of Malua Bay has been working towards helping Masaai women live safer lives in Kenya by raising funds to bring water to their villages. Thanks to her efforts and that of the Rotary Club of Batemans Bay, that dream is about to come true. Photos: Supplied.

How does a woman who lives in a comfortable seaside community like Malua Bay on the NSW South Coast know what women in a Masaai village in Kenya need – and enable $100,000 to be raised to help them?

For Sharlene Cohen, it’s simple: you listen.

It began when Sharlene embarked on a trip that changed her life – and, as it turns out, the lives of many other women.

Through the Thin Green Line organisation, which supports wildlife rangers globally, she travelled to Kenya where she met and formed connections with local women.

“It was after the bushfires here, and COVID,” she said, “and everything was standing still. It wasn’t like I went there for a holiday and came back with cause. I met a lot of people over there and those connections stayed strong so when I went back in 2022, I just reconnected with people.”

On her second visit she was invited to stay with Masaai women in their mud huts learning to understand, observe and listen. She also learned the language, thanks to hand signals and local children.

The Masaai women accepted Sharlene into their community, giving her a Masaai name, Namayiana, which means blessing.

Living with the women, Sharlene learned quickly that their biggest issue was water – safe and reliable access to it for more than 1000 people and their livestock.

Every day, the community’s women and girls would walk up to 12 kilometres, spending up to three hours in the baking sun just to collect water. When they got there, they often found the area to be unsafe or tightly controlled and where the taps or dams held no water.

This time taken from the women and girls’ school, income-earning work or family care was significant, especially, Sharlene said, as it was against Masaai culture for men to carry the water.

The women also faced the additional danger of wild elephants which frequented the watering holes.

“With reliable water close to home, that lost time can be transformed into education, livelihoods, and safer futures,” Sharlene said.

So the Masaai Mammas project, founded by Sharlene and supported by the Rotary Club of Batemans Bay, was born.

“The women told me they needed safe and reliable access to water, so that’s how the project started.

Sharlene Cohen outside her hut in the Kenyan village which bears her Masaai name, Namayiana which means “blessing”.

“Until you’re living alongside them, as I was, you don’t know how hard it is to carry 20 litres of water,” she said.

“The women approached me about it. I didn’t want to be the white saviour; it’s not about fixing people who don’t need it or telling people what to do. This is what they told me they needed.”

Coming from a farming background herself, Sharlene said she knew how valuable water was on the land and how having better access to it could help remedy myriad issues.

Thanks to the Rotary Club of Batemans Bay, the Masaai Mammas project has almost reached its goal of $100,000 to drill and install a 100-metre solar-powered borehole and shared wildlife and livestock water trough. This will deliver reliable water directly into four manyattas.

“We’re at $98,000,” Sharlene, who returns to Kenya next month when work is scheduled to start on the bores, said.

“We had to keep it quiet because we didn’t know how long it would take to raise the money. But when the villagers were told at a meeting that the water was coming, I can tell you there was a lot of singing and dancing.”

Although funds raised for the bore project are near the goal, the next project is for villagers to develop gardens where they can grow their own food once the bores are operating. Donations can be made through the Masaai Mammas website.

More information about the project is available here.

Original Article published by Sally Hopman on About Regional.

canberra.title: Spinning around Belco? Check out how this wall became a tribute to Aussie icons
canberra.snippet: Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave are icons of Australian music, and now they’re lighting up the back streets of Belconnen as the subject...
canberra.content:
Mural artist Lawrence Tan and his dog Midas have brought Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave to life in Hennessey Street, Belconnen. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave are icons of Australian music, and now they’re lighting up the back streets of Belconnen as the subject of a new house-side mural.

While a painting of two instantly recognisable musicians isn’t new, the way the mural was put together isn’t quite what you would expect, with a VR headset playing a major role in its creation.

The idea for the mural came after David, the owner of the house the mural is on, thought his home’s streetside wall looked a bit grim after removing the foliage around it.

To brighten the wall and add some colour, he turned to his friends, who recommended street artist Lawrence Tan.

Lawrence has painted over 50 murals across the ACT and NSW, but to help bring Kylie and Nick to life, Lawrence decided to use some new technology.

“I used my Meta Quest (VR headset) to map it out,” Lawrence said.

“We reached out to the original photographer of the image, Tony Mott, to get the copyright. I then uploaded it to this app on the headset.

“It allowed me to project the image onto the side of the walls. Traditionally, you would have to use a physical grid, a projector or some stencils. They all have limitations.

“For example, with a projector, you can only use it at night, or stencils are quite difficult to navigate. With the headset, I can use it at any time and still use both my hands.

“Once it’s mapped, I can walk up close to it, and the image sits there digitally like it’s been physically stencilled.”

Lawrence reached out to the original photographer Tony Mott for permission to use his iconic photo.

Lawrence said the tracing using the headset only took him an hour, compared to traditional methods that would have taken much longer.

Once mapped, it took Lawrence around 40 hours across several days to complete the artwork.

But now that the mural is complete, David said he couldn’t be happier with the result.

“I’ve always loved and admired Kylie. She’s been a constant in my life across her four-decade-long career,” David said.

“I find myself deliberately going outside each day to say hello to Kylie and Nick.

“I see the level of detail and the complexity of it, and it’s honestly so remarkable. It really is quite beautiful.”

David isn’t the only one blown away by the mural either.

“My neighbours actually wrote me a very nice card thanking me for the mural,” he said.

“It really is such a nice feeling that others have enjoyed seeing a little bit of colour in our part of Belconnen.

“For me, Kylie is such a family-oriented person who has a very special relationship with her sister and her brother. So for that image to bring this little part of the community together, it’s quite a nice feeling.”

australia.title: First H5 bird flu death of endangered Australian sea lion recorded amid fears for small population
australia.snippet: South Australian authorities say case discovered on Kangaroo Island is first for species of which less than 12,000 animals remain Get our...
australia.content:
South Australia has recorded the first death of an endangered Australian sea lion from H5 bird flu.

Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though a more recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000. Most of the population are found in South Australia, with the remainder in Western Australia.

On Sunday, the state’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the sea lion was found dead at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, the third-largest single colony.

“We’ve seen quite a number of mammal cases, but the Australian sea lion is the rarest seal found in our Australian waters,” Bourke said.

“85% of the population is found here in South Australia. It’s an endangered species.”

She said the sea lion had been recovering from a shark attack, but that bird flu had caused its death.

“We found that it was actually not the shark attack that killed the sea lion. It was the bird flu … we might find that this particular case was more susceptible because it was recovering.”

The government said the sea lion had first been observed with the shark wound three months ago and had been monitored since that time. Tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu and the government said it was confident the shark wound had not caused its death. There had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at Seal Bay, but the population was being closely monitored.

Bourke said there was “no real” mammal vaccine that “you could get off the shelf at the moment”.

“It was used in cattle in the US and they did an experimental trial in Hawaii on their monk seals, which they have seen that has been successful,” Bourke said.

“We have been working very closely with the federal government to highlight that we are willing and able to participate in a trial here in South Australia.”

Seal Bay has an estimated 800 Australian sea lions.

Bourke said the population was already diminishing by 2% every year, even before the arrival of bird flu, which will have a “devastating impact” on population levels if no vaccine can be administered.

“We’ve seen Heard Island [that there has been] a reduction in the population there for our seal pups by 75%. They were impacted by bird flu,” she said.

“And we’ve seen other experiences around the world where they were impacted by 95%. We know that this is going to be not the first and only case of [the virus] going into our sea lions.”

Last month, John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, told Guardian Australia that he feared the virus would quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.

“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.

“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.

“It’s likely in the next few weeks it will spread more quickly into the sea lion population in South Australia generally because of the proximity of the sea lion colonies to breeding seabird colonies or affected seabirds.”

H5 bird flu has already affected pinnipeds in South America and sub-Antarctica, where it has caused catastrophic losses in populations of some species, particularly among pups.

SA had confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal in August, after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.

australia.title: First case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion confirmed – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed. Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Hastie says he “feels sorry” for Barnaby Joy...
australia.content:
Confirmed case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion

Lisa Cox

South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion.

The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday.

The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu.

The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely.

Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia.

Scientists had warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica.

SA confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal in August after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.

John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said at the time he feared the virus could quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.

“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.

“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.”

Key events

  • 8h ago

    What we learned, Sunday 13 September

  • 10h ago

    Confirmed case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion

  • 11h ago

    Hanson faces bipartisan attack over resurfaced comments on Albanese’s mother

  • 11h ago

    Albanese criticises Hanson’s ‘spiteful’ comments about his mother using public housing

  • 11h ago

    Melissa Doyle appointed chair of Australia Day Council board

  • 12h ago

    Joyce and Farley having ‘buyer's remorse’, Hastie suggests

  • 12h ago

    Hanson ‘started a fight, and I intend to win it’, Hastie says

  • 13h ago

  • 13h ago

    WA police hunting for two men after shooting in Perth’s south-western suburbs

  • 13h ago

    Bowen: Conflict in Middle East will impact fuel prices in Australia

  • 13h ago

    Welcome

What we learned, Sunday 13 September

And with that, we are going to put the blog to bed. Before we go, let’s recap the big headlines.

  • Energy minister Chris Bowen sought to reassure Australians about the nation’s supply reserves. He said Australia had 41 days worth of petrol in strategic reserve and 42 days worth of diesel. But he warned the escalating conflict in Iran would impact fuel prices.

  • Speaking on Insiders, communications minister Anika Wells defended the opt-out push for social media algorithms, saying it was a “sensible measure to try and deal with these emerging harms that are coming”.

  • Television presenter Melissa Doyle has been appointed chair of the Australia Day Council board. She said: “I am honoured. I’m humbled. I’m daunted. I’m excited”.

  • Anthony Albanese said Pauline Hanson’s comments that it was “not on” that his mother lived in public housing for decades. The PM said: “If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that’s fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson’s league, way out of it.”

  • South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion. Scientists have warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population, which is endangered, if bird flu takes hold.

Thank you for spending some of your day with us. We will be back tomorrow to do it all again.

Sea lion dead from bird flu had been recovering from shark attack, minister says

The South Australian environment minister, Emily Bourke, has given an update on the first confirmed detection of H5 bird flu in an Australian sea lion.

Bourke said:

We’ve seen quite a number of mammal cases, but the Australian sea lion is the rarest … found in our Australian waters. Eighty-five per cent of the population is found here in South Australia.

It’s an endangered species, and today we are confirming our first case in this endangered species here in South Australia.

She said the sea lion was recovering from a shark attack, but bird flu had caused its death.

We found that it was actually not the shark attack that killed the sea lion. It was the bird flu case. We might find that this particular case was more susceptible because it was recovering.

Experts say about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain – though one recent estimate put the figure at less than 10,000.

Victoria launches ‘women’s pain standard’ for health practitioners

A women’s pain standard to set clear expectations for how health services recognise, assess and respond to pain has been launched following an inquiry that uncovered systemic failings, AAP has reported.

The Australian-first Victorian Women’s Pain Standard, announced on Sunday, will be embedded across the state’s public health services and aims to give women more consistent and higher-quality care.

It follows an inquiry into women’s pain in November where medical gender bias and healthcare system barriers were laid bare, which was leading to denial or dismissal of pain, misdiagnoses or delayed diagnoses.

The state government flagged it would develop a pain standard for women after the inquiry, which has now been created alongside clinicians, experts and women.

The South Australian government says there are three new detections of H5 bird flu, including the sea lion.

The other new cases are a greater crested tern at Port Noarlunga South, and a little penguin at Victor Harbor.

There have now been 290 confirmed cases of the virus in South Australia, from more than 2,000 tests administered by authorities.

Confirmed case of bird flu in endangered Australian sea lion

Lisa Cox

South Australia has confirmed its first H5 bird flu case in an endangered Australian sea lion.

The sea lion was found dead by a state government ranger at Seal Bay at Kangaroo Island on Friday.

The animal had sustained a shark wound three months prior and was already being monitored. The government said it was confident the shark wound was not the cause of death and tests had returned a strong positive result for H5 bird flu.

The government said there had been no other known endangered sea lion deaths at seal bay but it was monitoring the population closely.

Seal Bay has an estimated 800 resident Australian sea lions, the third largest single colony for the species and about 5% of the total population. About three quarters of Australia’s sea lion population lives in South Australia.

Scientists had warned of the potential “carnage” in the Australian sea lion population if bird flu takes hold, after the virus had already impacted seal populations in South America and sub-Antarctica.

SA confirmed Australia’s first case in a mainland mammal in August after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1.

John Woinarski, a leading mammal scientist at Charles Darwin University, said at the time he feared the virus could quickly start affecting more seals and sea lions.

“The carnage may be substantial and represent a serious conservation impact,” he said.

“I fear for Australian sea lions in particular because of their small population size.”

Victorian Labor pledges to recruit 1,500 additional police officers

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has said the government will recruit an extra 1,500 frontline police if elected. The election pledge also includes building a new training academy in Melbourne’s south-west.

He said:

We know we’ve got to get more police on the street, community safety is my number one priority. This comprehensive plan deals with the how. This is the difference between the Liberal-One Nation policy on police recruits and Labor’s policy.

Liberal-One Nation have promised more police. They’ve also said they’ll bring them from overseas. What Labor is promising is the pathway to unlock more police. With the second police academy to complement Glen Waverley.”

RBA expected to raise cash rate

Comments by senior Reserve Bank of Australia officials will be closely monitored as anticipation builds towards another interest rate hike later this month, AAP has reported.

The central bank’s chief economist, Sarah Hunter, will participate in a fireside chat at a Regional Australia Institute summit in Canberra on Monday.

Then, RBA governor Michele Bullock will appear before a parliamentary committee on Friday.

Both are expected to echo recent comments from bank officials reiterating that inflation is too high and leaving the door open to further interest rate hikes, after the three the bank has handed down so far in 2026.

Hunter and RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser sent bonds markets into a spin in separate hawkish speaking appearances last week.

Markets are now pricing in about a four in five chance the RBA will lift the cash rate by 25 basis points on 29 September.

Hanson faces bipartisan attack over resurfaced comments on Albanese’s mother

Krishani Dhanji

Pauline Hanson has come under fire from Liberal and Labor MPs for “appalling” comments attacking Anthony Albanese’s mother that have resurfaced from an old podcast interview.

The One Nation leader criticised Albanese’s mother, Maryanne Ellery, for staying in public housing for several decades, in a podcast with Karl Stefanovic from February this year.

Andrew Hastie, who has had his own fight with Hanson, this morning criticised Hanson and told News24 she should “leave mums out of it”.

I don’t think you should be talking about the late mother of anyone in this game, and certainly not reflecting on circumstances over which she had no understanding … I remember in the schoolyard, if anyone said anything about your mum, mate, it was on. So let’s leave mums out of it.”

The trade minister, Don Farrell, also berated Hanson for the remarks this morning, telling News24:

Anthony loves his mother, as I’m sure you do, I certainly loved my mother … To have them attacked publicly this way is just appalling. There’s a certain bitterness in One Nation’s approach to the world that I find quite un-Australian, actually. I think Ms Hanson should apologise.”

Albanese defends his mother as ‘way out of Pauline Hanson’s league’

The PM says he is “stunned at these comments”.

But I’ll make this point. If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that’s fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson’s league, way out of it.”

Albanese criticises Hanson’s ‘spiteful’ comments about his mother using public housing

The PM is back up where he is talking about comments Pauline Hanson made about his mother living in public housing. Hanson said in February it was “not on” that his mother had lived in public housing for decades, saying such housing “should be limited time”. This week she told the Australian, “The Prime Minister complains about his housing commission upbringing”.

In response, he said:

Firstly she made comments about me being complaining about being growing up in public housing. Nothing could be further from the truth. I’m proud to be a ‘houso’, and I’m proud of the community in which I grew up. I’m also proud about my mother.

She was someone who had a tough life. She didn’t associate with billionaires. She was someone who as has been documented, when overseas, came back to a Australia chose to make the courageous decision in 1963 to keep a child out of wedlock. Who is now the prime minister of Australia.

I said during the last campaign, kindness isn’t weakness. I’ll tell you what’s weakness – nastiness, and spitefulness.

Melissa Doyle is up now. She says:

I am honoured. I’m humbled. I’m daunted. I’m excited. I’m every single emotion. But above all, as a journalist, as a storyteller, I have spent my entire career telling the stories of people who inspire us heroes. We all need to hear about extraordinary people doing extraordinary things in our community, advocating for us all in so many fields, be it science, be it sport, be it art, be it community leaders.

I think we all need to hear those stories. And so to be able to play a role with the National Australia Day Council, to work with the board, to work with the executive, to continue to champion these extraordinary Australians and celebrate them and inspire all of us. Look, it’s truly an honour and I’m really excited.”

Albanese:

This is an important role for our nation. For decades, Australians have trusted Mel [Doyle] to tell Australian stories and now she will take that to the next level in the national interest. Australia Day is an important day where we come together.

Melissa Doyle appointed chair of Australia Day Council board

Anthony Albanese is speaking in Sydney, where he has just announced that television presenter Melissa Doyle has been appointed chair of the Australia Day Council board.

People in western NSW developing MND at four times global average

People across a vast swathe of Australia are developing a deadly disease at more than four times the global average, AAP has reported.

Researchers found a motor neurone disease (MND) incidence rate of 3.72 cases per 100,000 people annually across western NSW.

In some areas, the prevalence of MND was up to seven times higher than expected, with several higher-incidence regions overlapping with areas of more intensive agricultural activity.

The global burden of MND is increasing, and in 2021 the age-standardised prevalence and incidence were estimated at 0.77 cases per 100,000 people.

MND was also observed to be occurring at higher rates in women than in other areas, and the incidence of bulbar-onset MND was unusually high.

australia.title: Albanese hits back at Pauline Hanson’s ‘nastiness’ after criticism of his mother’s use of public housing
australia.snippet: Andrew Hastie also says One Nation leader is ‘not the person I thought she was’ and he feels sorry for Joyce Follow our Australia news li...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has labelled Pauline Hanson nasty and spiteful over resurfaced comments from the One Nation leader criticising his mother for living in public housing for decades.

Hanson also faced further a political threat from Liberal MP Andrew Hastie – who vowed to go “all the way” in his fight with her – as he suggested One Nation MPs Barnaby Joyce and David Farley were likely feeling buyers’ remorse for joining the party.

On Sunday, Albanese said he was “stunned” by Hanson’s comments, made in a February episode of Karl Stefanovic’s podcast, in which the One Nation leader criticised the length of time his mother lived in public housing. Hanson had also labelled the prime minister “pathetic” for repeatedly referencing his housing commission upbringing.

Albanese said he was “proud” of his “battler” mother, who died in 2002.

“I tell you what’s weakness: nastiness and spitefulness, and I am stunned at these comments,” he told reporters.

“But I’ll make this point: if Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that’s fine. But my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson’s league. Way out.”

The trade minister, Don Farrell, also lambasted Hanson over the “appalling” comments and called on the One Nation leader apologise.

“There’s a certain bitterness in One Nation’s approach to the world that I find quite un-Australian, actually. I think Ms Hanson should apologise,” Farrell told News24.

Hanson has been approached for comment.

In the podcast, Hanson referred to Albanese’s comments about his mother living in public housing “for 65 years” and said she believed it was “not on”.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years] – and he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years,” Hanson had said. “Sorry, that is not on, to me.”

“It should be limited time, you have been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through.”

Hastie vows to go ‘all the way’

It came as Hastie again accused Hanson of being a “lying coward”, after she continued to refuse to take down an animated cartoon that described him as a “traitor”. This came after he was subpoenaed to give evidence during Ben Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation trial.

“She’s still a lying coward. I’m not backing down,” Hastie told News24 on Sunday. “I put the challenge to her. She could have accepted that she’d got it wrong and pulled it down, but she refused to do so, and she has doubled down.

“I’ll go all the way with One Nation if they want … she started a fight, and I intend to win it.”

He also said he had previously tried to develop a relationship with Hanson, but that she is “not the person I thought she was”.

Hastie accepted Joyce’s apology to him over the cartoon video on Friday, who claimed he had not seen it. But the Liberal MP claimed his colleague, and One Nation MP David Farley, were likely having “buyers’ remorse” over joining the party.

“The whole party centres on her. I think this is why Barnaby Joyce and, I reckon, David Farley are probably having buyers’ remorse. They’re thinking, what did I get myself into?” Hastie said.

“I’ll say this about Barnaby Joyce. I feel sorry for the bloke, all right? He left a party that made him deputy prime minister twice, to jump in with this rabble, there’s no principles, they’re all over the shop, and he’s out there every week cleaning up after them.”

Joyce told Guardian Australia the assumption was “not correct” and defended his party.

“My fear is that the Coalition tread water rather than find land, and lack the strength to make difficult decisions. Politics is not a beauty pageant nor a reality tv show and we get more and more of that,” Joyce said.

“I am in One Nation because I am deeply concerned that the political status quo has become lazy and then weak.”

Farley has been approached for comment.

Hastie has been under attack from One Nation politically for several months, with the party announcing it would target his West Australian seat of Canning. The state seat of Secret Harbour, which One Nation won in a byelection last month, overlaps his federal electorate.

australia.title: NSW to put strict caps on screen time in classrooms while pushing for ‘pen and paper’ learning
australia.snippet: Screen limits will become mandatory in NSW schools from 2028 as federal education minister says students may need a ‘digital detox’ Follo...
australia.content:
The New South Wales government has announced it will implement limits on screen time in public school classrooms and push for students to take part in daily “pen and paper” learning.

The state’s new regulations follow a similar announcement from the Victorian government and suggestions by the federal education minister, Jason Clare, that students might need a “digital detox”.

Under the new regulations, Kindergarten to Year 2 students will be restricted to 15 minutes per day of learning on individual student devices, such as tablets or laptops.

Older children will be allowed additional time: up to 30 minutes a day for students in Years 3 and 4; and 45 minutes for Years 5 and 6.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

High school students will have restrictions based on their individual subject. In Years 7 to 10, the use of personal digital devices will be limited to a quarter of subject time; senior high school students will be allowed to use devices for up to half their learning time.

The government also says there would be new guidelines that limit the use of screens for homework, including not recommending any such use for children younger than Year 5.

Guidelines will also recommend “a minimum of one hour a day” be devoted to pen and paper learning.

The screen limits will be recommended next year and become mandatory in NSW schools from 2028.

The state’s education minister, Prue Car, said the government’s research “is telling us that excessive screen use is a problem”. She said parents wanted screens to be used intentionally, rather than as a default.

“An entire generation of students [is] increasingly living in an online world,” Car said.

“We have a responsibility to ensure their health and education isn’t impacted by excessive screen use.

“We have already seen positive results from our ban on mobile phones, with fewer distractions in class and improved engagement.

“When the research is telling us students are spending as much as seven hours a day on screens, and we are seeing reading and writing skills go backwards for a whole generation of children, we have to act.”

The government announcement included a statement by the state’s chief paediatrician, Dr Helen Goodwin, who said too much time on screens impacts important daily activities that support healthy growth and development.

In a statement, the government said digital literacy would remain a part of the curriculum, but that the policy aimed to “reduce the cumulative impact of screen time” on students’ development.

Screen limits have been pushed by some teacher and parent groups.

australia.title: Do not call her a racist: anti-Pauline Hanson strategists tell campaigners character attacks won’t work in Victoria
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Strategic rethink urges progressive activists to respectfully steer one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters toward...
australia.content:
The message from strategists was blunt: do not, however tempting, personally attack Pauline Hanson or call her a racist.

The request has been made to progressive campaigners and unionists who have been asked to start one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters before the Victorian election in November.

It is also indicative of a strategic rethink in response to One Nation’s sustained surge in public support and the party’s recent wins in state and federal byelections and in South Australia.

Separate training sessions run by the peak body for unions in Victoria, the Trades Hall Council, and the progressive campaign group GetUp, have warned members they may be inadvertently pushing people to One Nation by not respectfully engaging with their legitimate economic concerns.

“As best as you can, I know it’s hard, don’t make it personal,” a GetUp strategist told hundreds of members on a Thursday night Zoom call.

“Going after Pauline Hanson personally and calling her a racist, or going after her character, although very tempting, just confirms what people already believe: that she is an outsider and the establishment is attacking her.”

This is a change of approach for the progressive group, which spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads personally attacking Hanson and her deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, during the Farrer byelection. The ads, which linked the pair to Donald Trump, had little impact. One Nation comfortably won the seat.

The reset, based on research conducted by the polling company Redbridge after the Farrer byelection, brought GetUp in line with advice from Trades Hall, which has been hosting training sessions for major unions in recent weeks.

Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett, a senior researcher at Trades Hall, says people thinking about voting for One Nation shut down when they perceive personal attacks on the party’s leadership that do not acknowledge their legitimate concerns.

“For many people, simply ignoring her racism is not going to be possible or desirable,” Kaspi-Crutchett said. “It’s what drives them to get involved in the fight against One Nation.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“In these cases, we need to make it very clear that Hanson’s racism isn’t merely a character flaw but a sophisticated political device. It manufactures differences between groups which have none.”

GetUp has also told campaigners to not personally attack Hanson’s billionaire benefactor.

“Pauline Hanson is closely tied to Gina Rinehart, and it’s a problem, but it’s not what the research says should be in focus,” GetUp told campaigners.

“It can be effective if it is raised organically by the person you’re speaking to but leading with it reads as a standard partisan attack, which triggers the same defensiveness as going after her character directly.”

This advice marks another change for the group, which in the weeks after the Farrer byelection published ads describing Hanson as a “wannabe billionaire” flying around in “mummy Gina’s” private plane.

Senior state and federal Labor sources, who declined to be named so they could speak freely, say these changes makes sense. They argue the group’s personal attacks on rightwing figures, including Peter Dutton during the 2016 and 2019 federal elections, were not helpful.

GetUp’s decision to unveil a banner behind Hanson during her National Press Club address in June caused disquiet among Labor ranks, with some arguing it was unproductive. While the banner’s message focused on her record on wages, it also included cartoon images of cash flying around her.

‘Listen to the beat, not the lyrics’

Kaspi-Crutchett and his colleagues at Trades Hall are telling unionists to listen carefully for any hint of economic concerns that may be underpinning opinions about immigration, crime or culture wars.

“Pauline Hanson’s greatest weaknesses and the policy areas where she is the most vulnerable are the ones where the Labor movement has the highest trust from the public: working conditions, entitlements, maternity leave,” he says.

He says campaigners should resist the urge to factcheck conspiracy theories. Instead, conversations should be respectfully redirected to the economy.

“Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying,” he says. “What is consistent is their dissatisfaction with the status quo so get them to tease out what that looks like and how it makes them feel.

“There might be a spiel about Bill Gates but, eventually, you get to them saying ‘my kid can’t afford a house’.”

In June, the head of Trades Hall Council, Luke Hilakari, rebuked 23 state Labor MPs and candidates for having “zero conversations” with their constituents in the past two weeks, saying they needed to “work their ass off” to stop One Nation.

Kaspi-Crutchett said one-on-one conversations are vital because the politicians that once persuaded people against voting for Hanson had “lost credibility with the people she is targeting”.

“A nurse on the doorstep can do infinitely more than a legion of cabinet ministers and press secretaries.” Kaspi-Crutchett said.

“The trust has been exhausted.”

world.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
world.snippet: Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba ...
world.content:
Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.

Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.

Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.

He died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.

Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.

At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.

“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.

Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.

The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.

A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.

But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.

Supporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.

A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.

The archbishop of the ⁠Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.

“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he ​told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy ​of the king we are mourning.”

Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.

In ​addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning ‌against HIV and Aids, ​Oyo cultivated close ties with former ​Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.

The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a low profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.

Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.

world.title: Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6m online romance scam
world.snippet: Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa Six Nigerian nationals linked to ...
world.content:
Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.

South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.

The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges.

They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams.

According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.

Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.

“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.

A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.

The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.

In South Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.

In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.

world.title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide
world.snippet: Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against ...
world.content:
Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.

The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.

Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.

The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.

The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.

Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”

UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.

Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.

“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.

Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.

In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.

The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.

Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.

“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”

She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”

Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.

“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.

“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”

FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.

A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

world.title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom
world.snippet: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch A traditional ...
world.content:
A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.

On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.

However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.

The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”

In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.

She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.”

Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.

“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.

Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities.

The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.

Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.

The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.

“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”

Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.

Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.

Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.

In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.

The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
world.snippet: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’ Uganda is withdrawing f...
world.content:
Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.

Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.

When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”

The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.

The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”

The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.

The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.

Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.

The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.
